claims.text: Introducing a controlled volume fraction of a ductile BCC precipitate phase can increase ductility in the refractory HEA.
The ductile BCC precipitate phase can make deformation more uniform.
The ductility improvement can occur without compromising high strength.
The ductility improvement can occur without compromising impact-induced energy release.
Powder-metallurgy-processed NbMoCrTiAl has a room-temperature compressive fracture strength of approximately 1500 MPa.
The reinforced NbMoCrTiAl composite exhibits cleavage fracture with negligible room-temperature ductility.
The brittle behavior of the NbMoCrTiAl composite is caused by its TiC and Al2O3 reinforcements.
Changing ball-milling duration or spark-plasma-sintering conditions can promote in-situ formation of a nanoscale ductile BCC precipitate phase.
A minor alloying addition can promote in-situ formation of a nanoscale ductile BCC precipitate phase.
The prior NbMoCrTiAl processing route used high-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering.
The desired BCC precipitates will be nanoscale and uniformly distributed at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
The ductile BCC phase will blunt cracks.
The ductile BCC phase will accommodate dislocations and provide pathways for plastic deformation.
Plastic accommodation by the ductile phase will reduce stress concentrations and hinder cleavage propagation.
The treated material will have greater strain to fracture than the untreated composite.
The treated material will exhibit more homogeneous plastic deformation than the untreated composite.
The untreated composite contains substantial fractions of TiC and Al2O3 particles.
An overly coarse or excessive ductile phase may reduce second-phase strengthening and compromise energy absorption.
